questions.q: Why does this lesson say a hallucination eval run once in Chapter 2 isn't enough once an AI system is in production?
options: Real production traffic isn't the fixed eval set — a model that scored well in testing can still generate an unsupported claim on a question nobody tested
Hallucinations only happen during the evaluation phase, never in production
Production traffic is always identical to the eval dataset
A one-time eval automatically re-runs itself against every new production request
questions.explain: Production traffic covers cases the fixed eval set never anticipated, so a passing eval score doesn't guarantee no hallucinations will occur on real traffic.

questions.q: What is a 'scorer,' as defined in this lesson?
options: A function, often an LLM-as-judge, that runs against a call's input and output and attaches a score or label to it automatically
A person manually grading every single AI response by hand
A fixed dollar amount charged for every flagged hallucination
A setting that deletes any response suspected of hallucinating
questions.explain: A scorer is an automated function — often an LLM-as-judge — that evaluates a call and attaches a result, allowing checks like hallucination detection to run continuously.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say seeing scorer results as columns across many calls at once matters more than looking at one scored call alone?
options: Single calls are always more informative than any aggregate view
Aggregate scores across calls are purely decorative and have no operational use
A pattern — like one prompt template generating more flagged responses than others — only becomes visible when you see scores across many calls, not just one
Looking at calls individually is illegal under AI regulations
questions.explain: A single scored call tells you about one response, but seeing scores across the whole traces table reveals patterns tied to specific templates or model versions.

questions.q: What does filtering a trace table by a scorer's output actually accomplish, according to this lesson?
options: It permanently deletes all unflagged calls from the system
It turns a monitoring signal into an actual worklist — isolating just the calls worth a human reviewing
It disables the scorer so it stops running on new calls
It automatically rewrites flagged responses to remove hallucinations
questions.explain: Filtering down to only the flagged calls is what makes a scorer operationally useful, rather than just a column of numbers nobody acts on.

questions.q: What does a predefined hallucination scorer specifically check, per this lesson?
options: Whether the response arrived within a set latency threshold
Whether the response's claims are actually supported by the context the model had access to
Whether the response used the cheapest available model
Whether the user who sent the request was logged in
questions.explain: A hallucination scorer evaluates whether claims in the output are grounded in the available context, rather than fabricated.
